title: Procrastinate for Success: why an overwhelmed founder should deliberately ignore most tasks
summary: Jason argues that in an overwhelmed small company, gut-feel procrastination can beat formal prioritization. Many problems resolve themselves, many tasks matter less than they seem, and batching low-value chores frees time for the one or two things that win. He also says to allow some fun to avoid burnout.

principles.text: You can't do everything, so deliberately put things off and don't feel guilty about it.
principles.quote: Yeah I know I'm rationalizing. But you can't do everything, so don't.

principles.text: Many urgent-seeming items resolve themselves if you just ignore them: features, customer demands, bugs, meetings, emails.
principles.quote: Many things blow over if you just ignore them. The big feature you got worked up about yesterday seems unimportant in the cold light of today.

principles.text: Even critical-sounding admin like accounting can wait; the cost is smaller than the revenue from one more customer.
principles.quote: Late fees, lost receipts, penalties from the IRS: financial burdens more than compensated by additional revenue gained by signing up one more customer.

principles.text: Batch repetitive chores into one sweep to avoid context-switch overhead and get faster.
principles.quote: It's faster to enter 100 receipts into Quickbooks once a month than to enter three a day.

principles.text: Companies win by getting a few things really right, not by having no flaws, so skip details to focus on the 1-2 most important things.
principles.quote: Companies succeed because they got just a few things really right, not because they had no problems, no bugs, no design flaws, and perfect books.

principles.text: Let yourself do some fun work; burnout costs more than the duties you put off.
principles.quote: Whatever the cost of putting off duties, burn-out is even more costly.
